planting.note: Divide offsets in spring or early fall; heuffelii types do not form true chicks on stolons.

directions: Set rosettes with the crown level with the soil surface in sharply draining, gritty soil. Expect red rosettes with a lime-green center through the growing season, deepening toward near-black purple once cold weather sets in. Long cilia fringe the leaf margins year-round. Water sparingly and avoid overhead irrigation that can trap moisture in the rosette.

common_name: Chick Charms Mint Chocolate Chip Hens and Chicks

planting.note: Patented Chick Charms selection (bred by Chris Hansen); propagate only by purchased offsets, not unlicensed division for resale.

directions: Grow in lean, fast-draining soil with full sun exposure to develop the strongest color banding. In warm weather foliage runs green-dominant with burgundy tips; the pattern reverses in cool weather, turning deep burgundy with green tips. Color intensity shifts noticeably with the seasons and with sun exposure. Remove spent mother rosettes after they bloom and die back to make room for new offsets.

common_name: Colorockz Coconut Crystal Hens and Chicks
directions: Plant in rock gardens, troughs, or rooftop plantings with gritty, low-fertility soil. Spring growth opens lime green with red highlights along pointed leaf tips, fading over the season to a cream-and-wine-red combination by summer heat. A fine silvery edge rims each leaf, giving the rosette a frosted look in bright light. Reduce watering sharply once established, since wet crowns in winter are the main cause of rot.

Grow in full sun in a fast-draining succulent mix to bring out the strongest coloring. Spoon-shaped leaves run from silvery blue-green to olive at the base, flushing lavender, pink, or near-red along the edges under bright light and seasonal cold. Rosettes slowly bulk up to roughly 8 inches across, with leaf tips folding gently upward. Bring indoors or under cover whenever temperatures threaten to drop near freezing.

planting.note: Robert Campbell hybrid (Echeveria 'Joy's Giant' x E. laui); handle farina-coated leaves gently.

directions: Site in bright, dry conditions where the wavy, paddle-shaped leaves can keep their natural powdery farina coating intact. Foliage reads silvery blue in heat and humidity but blushes rose-pink as nights cool or water is withheld. Mature clumps send up branched stalks of coral to orange-red flowers above the foliage. Avoid touching the leaf surface, since the waxy bloom rubs off and will not regenerate.

Grow in full sun and lean soil to push the rosette toward its signature purple-and-cocoa-brown tones; shaded plants stay greener and less frilled. Mature outer leaves develop ruffled edges and occasional small bumps, while new center growth emerges flat and silvery green by contrast. Over time the rosette can reach roughly 14 to 16 inches across before rising on a bare stem. Protect from frost, moving container plants indoors to a bright window when a freeze is forecast.

planting.note: Hybrid of Echeveria derenbergii x E. prolifica.

directions: Plant in shallow, well-drained containers since this compact hybrid offsets quickly into dense clumps. Triangular grey-blue leaves carry a red edge and a powdery farina coating that intensifies the color contrast in bright light. Mature clumps send up tall stalks of small, bell-shaped yellow flowers in late winter or spring. Keep rainfall off the rosettes where possible to prevent water spotting the farina.

planting.note: Interspecific hybrid with Dudleya caespitosa as one parent; keep bone dry through summer dormancy.

directions: Tuck into rocky slopes, raised beds, or containers with sharp drainage and some afternoon shade in hot inland gardens. Slender, finger-like silver leaves form dense mounds and take on a purple-red blush once winter chill arrives. Withhold summer water almost entirely, since this hybrid rests through the dry season and rots quickly if kept moist. Watch labels carefully at nurseries, as this hybrid is sometimes sold under the synonym 'Anacapa'.

planting.note: Orostachys japonica hybrid named for breeder Ed "Crazy Ed" Skrocki.

directions: Use a gritty, sharply drained rock-garden mix in full to part sun. Fleshy green rosettes roughly 5 inches wide offset readily like hens and chicks, knitting into a patch up to a foot and a half across over time. Established clumps send up spikes of white to cream, star-shaped flowers in fall before the flowering rosettes die back. Leave spent rosettes in place through winter, since new offsets continue to fill in around them the following season.

planting.note: Steve Jankalski hybrid of Graptopetalum paraguayense x G. superbum.

directions: Grow in full sun and lean, gritty soil, allowing the plant to go slightly stressed for the best color. Base leaf color runs glaucous grey-green with a waxy farina coating, developing raspberry-purple blotches that deepen into a hazy violet cast under strong light. Reduce water and increase sun exposure to intensify the purple tones further. Handle carefully, since farina rubs off the leaf surface and does not return once removed.
